```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown
from _lib.orplot import shade_polygon, convex_hull, mark_point, COLORS
from _lib.toy_benders import (C, XL, XU, PIECES, X_INT, f, classic_benders,
                              integer_optimum, master_lp)

LOG = classic_benders()
X_LP, T_LP, LB_LP = LOG[-1]["x"], LOG[-1]["t"], LOG[-1]["lb"]
X_IP, Z_IP = integer_optimum()
XS = np.linspace(XL, XU, 400)
FX = np.array([f(x) for x in XS])
T_TOP = 10.5

def cut_label(a, g):
    if g == 0:
        return f"$t \\geq {a:g}$"
    return f"$t \\geq {a:g} - {g:g}x$" if g != 1 else f"$t \\geq {a:g} - x$"

def axes_xt(ax):
    ax.set_xlim(XL - 0.2, XU + 0.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, T_TOP)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$t$")
    ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.5, alpha=0.5)
```

## The idea

Many large optimization models have a few **complicating variables** that, once fixed,
leave behind a problem that is easy to solve. In facility location, deciding *which*
facilities to open is hard (it is a discrete choice), but once that is fixed, assigning
customers to the open facilities is just a linear program. In two-stage stochastic
programming, once the here-and-now decision is fixed, each scenario's recourse problem
is a separate LP.

@benders1962 turned this observation into an algorithm. Instead of solving everything
at once, keep only the complicating variables $x$ in a **master problem** and replace the
rest by a single number $t$ that stands for "the cost of the easy part". The master does
not know that cost function exactly. It learns it a piece at a time from a
**subproblem**, which, given a proposed $x$, solves the easy LP and answers with a
**cut**, a linear inequality that tells the master what it got wrong. LP duality is what
makes these cuts exact.

## The problem and its subproblem

We use the notation of @fang2026. The problem is a mixed-integer linear program

$$
\min_{x,\,y}\; c^\top x + d^\top y
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad A x + B y \ge b,\qquad x \in X,
$$

where $X$ collects the bounds, the remaining constraints on $x$, and the integrality
requirements. The $y$ variables are continuous. Fixing $x = \hat x$ leaves the
**subproblem**

$$
f(\hat x) \;=\; \min_{y}\,\{\, d^\top y \;:\; B y \ge b - A\hat x \,\},
$$

a plain LP whose optimal value $f(\hat x)$ is the cost of the easy part for that choice
of $x$ ($f(\hat x) = +\infty$ if it is infeasible). The function $f$ is the
**value function** of the subproblem, and the original problem is simply

$$
\min_{x \in X}\; c^\top x + f(x).
$$

## The key result: projecting out $y$ with LP duality

The dual of the subproblem is

$$
f(\hat x) \;=\; \max_{\pi \in \Pi}\; (b - A\hat x)^\top \pi,
\qquad
\Pi = \{\, \pi \ge 0 \;:\; B^\top \pi = d \,\}.
$$

The crucial observation is that **$\Pi$ does not depend on $\hat x$**; only the objective
does. So the same finite list of extreme points $J$ and extreme rays $R$ of $\Pi$
describes the subproblem for every $x$:

- If some extreme ray $\tilde\pi \in R$ has $(b - A\hat x)^\top \tilde\pi > 0$, the dual is
  unbounded, so the subproblem is **infeasible** at $\hat x$.
- Otherwise the dual optimum is attained at an extreme point, and
  $f(\hat x) = \max_{\hat\pi \in J} (b - A\hat x)^\top \hat\pi$.

So $f$ is a maximum of finitely many affine functions: it is **convex and piecewise
linear**, with one linear piece per dual extreme point. Writing $t \ge f(x)$ gives the
**Benders reformulation**, an equivalent problem in $(x, t)$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x \in X,\; t}\quad & c^\top x + t \\
\text{s.t.}\quad & t \ge \hat\pi^\top (b - A x) && \forall\, \hat\pi \in J
   \qquad \text{(optimality cuts)} \\
& 0 \ge \tilde\pi^\top (b - A x) && \forall\, \tilde\pi \in R
   \qquad \text{(feasibility cuts)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Following @fang2026, call the set of $(x, t)$ satisfying all these cuts $L$. It is the
epigraph of $f$ restricted to the $x$ for which the subproblem is feasible, and the
problem is $\min\{c^\top x + t : (x,t) \in L,\; x \in X\}$. This equivalence is the
partitioning theorem of @benders1962.

The reformulation has a catch: $J$ and $R$ can be exponentially large, so the cuts can't
be written down in advance. Benders decomposition generates them **only when needed**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why every optimality cut is valid (weak duality)
Take any $\hat\pi \in \Pi$ and any $x$ for which the subproblem is feasible, with optimal
solution $y^*$. Then $\hat\pi \ge 0$ and $B y^* \ge b - Ax$ give
$$
\hat\pi^\top (b - A x) \;\le\; \hat\pi^\top B y^* \;=\; (B^\top \hat\pi)^\top y^* \;=\; d^\top y^* \;=\; f(x).
$$
So $t \ge \hat\pi^\top(b - Ax)$ never cuts off a pair $(x, t)$ with $t \ge f(x)$: it is a
valid underestimator of $f$, and it is *tight* at the point where $\hat\pi$ is
dual-optimal. Feasibility cuts follow the same way from Farkas' lemma [@farkas1902]:
if $\tilde\pi \ge 0$, $B^\top\tilde\pi = 0$ and $\tilde\pi^\top(b - Ax) > 0$, then
$B y \ge b - Ax$ has no solution.
:::

### A tiny example

Throughout this page we use a one-dimensional problem, small enough to draw:

$$
\min\; 2.5\,x + f(x), \qquad x \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\},
\qquad
f(x) = \min_y \{\, y \;:\; y \ge 9 - 4x,\; y \ge 5 - x,\; y \ge 0 \,\}.
$$

Here $d = 1$, $B = (1, 1, 1)^\top$ and $b - Ax = (9 - 4x,\; 5 - x,\; 0)^\top$, so
$\Pi = \{\pi \ge 0 : \pi_1 + \pi_2 + \pi_3 = 1\}$. Its three extreme points are the unit
vectors, and they give the three optimality cuts $t \ge 9 - 4x$, $t \ge 5 - x$ and
$t \ge 0$. The subproblem is always feasible, so there are no feasibility cuts.

```{python}
#| label: fig-value-function
#| fig-cap: "The value function $f$ of the example (black) is the upper envelope of three affine functions, one per extreme point of the dual feasible region (dashed). The shaded region is $L$, the epigraph of $f$, which the Benders reformulation describes with cuts."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
axes_xt(ax)
shade_polygon(ax, list(zip(XS, FX)) + [(XU, T_TOP), (XL, T_TOP)], "#888888", alpha=0.15, lw=0)
for (a, g), col in zip(PIECES, [COLORS["p1"], COLORS["p2"], COLORS["hull"]]):
    ax.plot(XS, a - g * XS, ls="--", color=col, lw=1.4, label=cut_label(a, g))
ax.plot(XS, FX, color="black", lw=2.2, label="$f(x)$")
ax.text(3.0, 7.5, "$L$ = epigraph of $f$", fontsize=10)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

## The algorithm

Start the master problem with a few cuts (or just a lower bound on $t$) and repeat:

1. **Solve the master** with the cuts found so far. Its solution $(\hat x, \hat t)$ is the
   master's best guess, and its optimal value is a **lower bound** on the true optimum,
   since the master is a relaxation.
2. **Solve the subproblem** at $\hat x$ (in practice, its dual):
   - *infeasible* → add the **feasibility cut** $0 \ge \tilde\pi^\top (b - Ax)$ from the
     dual ray that proves it;
   - *$f(\hat x) > \hat t$* → the master underestimated the cost; add the **optimality
     cut** $t \ge \hat\pi^\top(b - Ax)$ from the optimal dual solution $\hat\pi$;
   - *$f(\hat x) \le \hat t$* → $(\hat x, \hat t) \in L$; the master's guess is correct and
     it is optimal for the current master problem. Stop.
3. Each feasible $\hat x$ also gives an **upper bound** $c^\top \hat x + f(\hat x)$.

Because each cut comes from one of finitely many extreme points or rays, and a cut once
added is never violated again, the loop ends after finitely many iterations
[@benders1962]. The figure runs it on the continuous relaxation $0 \le x \le 4$ of the
example, starting from the trivial cut $t \ge 0$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-benders-loop
#| fig-cap: "Classical Benders decomposition on the LP relaxation of the example. In each panel: the true value function $f$ (grey), the master's current approximation, the upper envelope of the cuts found so far (blue), the master solution $(\\hat x, \\hat t)$ (red), and the subproblem's answer $f(\\hat x)$ (black). The dashed line is the cut the subproblem returns. In the last panel the master's point lies on $f$, so the loop stops."
n = len(LOG)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n, figsize=(3.6 * n, 3.6), sharey=True)
for ax, it in zip(axes, LOG):
    axes_xt(ax)
    ax.plot(XS, FX, color="#999999", lw=2.0)
    env = np.max([[a - g * x for x in XS] for a, g in it["cuts"]], axis=0)
    ax.plot(XS, env, color=COLORS["p1"], lw=2.0)
    if it["new_cut"] is not None:
        a, g = it["new_cut"]
        ax.plot(XS, a - g * XS, ls="--", color="black", lw=1.2)
        ax.plot([it["x"], it["x"]], [it["t"], it["fx"]], color=COLORS["weak"], lw=1, ls=":")
        mark_point(ax, (it["x"], it["fx"]), "black", size=35)
    mark_point(ax, (it["x"], it["t"]), COLORS["weak"], size=55)
    title = f"Iteration {it['k'] + 1}"
    title += f"\nadd {cut_label(*it['new_cut'])}" if it["new_cut"] else "\n$(\\hat x,\\hat t) \\in L$: stop"
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-benders-loop
#| tbl-cap: "Iterations of the loop. The lower bound is the master's optimal value; the upper bound is the best $2.5\\,\\hat x + f(\\hat x)$ seen so far."
rows = []
for it in LOG:
    cut = cut_label(*it["new_cut"]) if it["new_cut"] else "— (stop)"
    rows.append(f"| {it['k'] + 1} | {it['x']:.3f} | {it['t'] + 0.0:.3f} | {it['fx']:.3f} | "
                f"{it['lb']:.3f} | {it['ub']:.3f} | {cut} |")
Markdown("| Iteration | $\\hat x$ | $\\hat t$ | $f(\\hat x)$ | Lower bound | Upper bound | Cut added |\n"
         "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

The cut added in iteration 1 is exact where it was generated ($t = f(0) = 9$ at $x = 0$)
and remains a valid underestimate everywhere else. After two cuts the master already
"knows" every piece of $f$ that matters, and the bounds meet at
`{python} f"{LB_LP:.2f}"`, the optimum of the **LP relaxation**, at the fractional point
$\hat x = 4/3$.

## Benders decomposition for mixed-integer programs

When $x$ must be integer, the master is a MILP, and there are two standard ways to
organize the loop. @fang2026 call them **BendersSeq** and **BendersBnB**:

- **BendersSeq** — the original scheme of @benders1962: solve the master MILP to
  optimality, call the subproblem, add a cut, and solve the master MILP again. It is
  simple, but every iteration solves a MILP from scratch.
- **BendersBnB (branch-and-Benders-cut)** — build a *single* branch-and-bound tree
  [@land1960] for the master and add Benders cuts as lazy constraints whenever the tree
  finds an integer candidate (and, optionally, at fractional nodes). This avoids
  re-solving the master and is usually much faster on large problems
  [@fortz2009; @fischetti2017; see the survey @rahmaniani2017].

Two structural variants are worth knowing:

- In **two-stage stochastic programming**, the subproblem separates into one LP per
  scenario. Benders decomposition there is known as the **L-shaped method**
  [@vanslyke1969]. Adding one cut per scenario instead of a single aggregated cut is the
  **multicut** version [@birge1988].
- When the subproblem is a convex nonlinear program instead of an LP, LP duality is
  replaced by nonlinear convex duality: **generalized Benders decomposition**
  [@geoffrion1972].

### Making it faster

Classical Benders decomposition is famous for being easy to state and hard to make
fast. Two classical accelerations:

- **Pareto-optimal cuts.** When the subproblem dual has several optimal solutions, they
  give different cuts, and some dominate others. @magnanti1981 showed how to choose,
  among the alternative dual optima, a cut that is not dominated.
- **In-out stabilization.** Instead of separating the master's solution itself, separate
  a point on the segment between it and an interior "core" point. Early iterations
  then zigzag less [@benameur2007]. It has been very effective, for example in
  large-scale facility location [@fischetti2017].

@rahmaniani2017 survey these and many other enhancements.

## Limits of classical Benders cuts {#limits}

The subproblem never sees the integrality of $x$, so every classical Benders cut is a
valid inequality for $L$, the **continuous** relaxation, and the best it can do is be
tight for $L$. @fang2026 put this limitation at the center of their paper
**[Disjunctive Benders Decomposition](papers/fang-2026.qmd)**. What the integer problem
needs are cuts for the much smaller set
$\mathrm{conv}\big((X \times \mathbb{R}) \cap L\big)$, the convex hull of the points of $L$
whose $x$ is integer. When the gap between the two sets is large, classical Benders
decomposition must rely on branching (BendersBnB) or on enumerating candidates
(BendersSeq) to close it. @fang2026 conjecture that this is a major cause of the
familiar **tail-off** of Benders decomposition: fast progress in the first iterations,
then many iterations that barely improve the bound.

Our example shows the effect in its simplest form. The LP relaxation stops at
$(\hat x, \hat t) = (4/3,\; 11/3)$, a point **on** the graph of $f$, so it lies in $L$. No
Benders cut, from any oracle, can ever cut it off. The integer problem, however, only
uses the points of $L$ above $x \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$, and their convex hull (green
below) is strictly smaller.

```{python}
#| label: fig-benders-limit
#| fig-cap: "The limit of Benders cuts. Grey: $L$, the region that classical Benders cuts describe. Green: $\\mathrm{conv}((X \\times \\mathbb{R}) \\cap L)$, the convex hull of the part of $L$ above integer $x$. The LP optimum (red) lies on the boundary of $L$, so no Benders cut can separate it. The dashed line is a cut valid for the green set, obtained from the disjunction $x \\le 1 \\lor x \\ge 2$; it removes the red point and closes the gap. (A one-dimensional analogue of the illustrations in @fang2026.)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.2))
axes_xt(ax)
shade_polygon(ax, list(zip(XS, FX)) + [(XU, T_TOP), (XL, T_TOP)], "#888888", alpha=0.35, lw=0)
ax.plot(XS, FX, color="black", lw=1.6)
int_pts = [(x, f(x)) for x in X_INT]
hull = convex_hull(int_pts + [(XL, T_TOP), (XU, T_TOP)])
shade_polygon(ax, hull, COLORS["hull"], alpha=0.30)
ax.annotate("part of $L$ outside\nthe convex hull", (1.3, 4.05), xytext=(0.15, 1.2),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#555555"), fontsize=9, color="#555555")
ax.scatter(*zip(*int_pts), color="black", s=30, zorder=6)
ax.plot(XS, 7 - 2 * XS, ls="--", color=COLORS["hull"], lw=1.8)
ax.annotate("disjunctive cut\n$t \\geq 7 - 2x$", (3.1, 0.8), xytext=(3.25, 4.6),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["hull"]), color="#2f6b3c", fontsize=9)
mark_point(ax, (X_LP, T_LP), COLORS["weak"], size=70)
ax.annotate("LP optimum\n$(4/3,\\ 11/3)$", (X_LP, T_LP), xytext=(1.75, 6.5),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["text"]), fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-benders-limit
#| tbl-cap: "Lower bounds for the example. The integer optimum is at $x = 1$."
(x_c, t_c), lb_cut = master_lp([p for p in PIECES], extra=[(7.0, 2.0)])
Markdown(
    "| Relaxation | Lower bound |\n|---|---:|\n"
    f"| Master with **all** Benders cuts (= LP relaxation) | {LB_LP:.2f} |\n"
    f"| Same, plus the disjunctive cut $t \\geq 7 - 2x$ | {lb_cut:.2f} |\n"
    f"| Integer optimum | {Z_IP:.2f} |"
)
```

Even with *every* Benders cut, the master's LP relaxation stays at
`{python} f"{LB_LP:.2f}"`, and only branching on $x$ can close the gap to the integer
optimum `{python} f"{Z_IP:.2f}"`. A single cut that "knows" $x$ is integer closes it
immediately. The dashed cut comes from the split $x \le 1 \lor x \ge 2$, exactly the
kind of [disjunctive cut](../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/solving.qmd)
used in integer programming.

The motivating example in @fang2026 makes the same point at a larger scale. Their
feasible set is a $51 \times 2$ integer grid with only two feasible points. Both
BendersSeq and BendersBnB, equipped with a state-of-the-art oracle, end up exploring
more than a quarter of the grid before proving optimality, while cuts for the convex
hull would finish almost immediately. (See the
[paper notes](papers/fang-2026.qmd) for details.)

### Other well-known difficulties

The integrality gap is not the only problem. The survey of @rahmaniani2017 discusses
others, including:

- **An expensive master.** BendersSeq solves a MILP in every iteration.
- **Weak or redundant cuts.** Degenerate subproblems have many dual optima. A careless
  choice gives weak cuts, which is the motivation for Pareto-optimal cuts
  [@magnanti1981].
- **Zigzagging.** Early master solutions jump around the domain, which motivates
  stabilization such as the in-out method [@benameur2007].

### Bringing integrality into the cuts

Several lines of work try to put the integrality of $x$ back into Benders cuts:

- **Mixed-integer rounding** applied to Benders cuts that were already generated
  [@bodurluedtke2017].
- **Split cuts** for stochastic integer programs, either in the extended space
  ("cut-and-project") or in the Benders reformulation ("project-and-cut")
  [@bodur2017].
- **Lagrangian cuts**, which add integrality to the subproblem through copies of the
  master variables [@zou2019; @rahmaniani2020].
- **Disjunctive Benders decomposition** [@fang2026], which builds cuts valid for
  $\mathrm{conv}\big((X \times \mathbb{R}) \cap L\big)$ by combining disjunctive
  programming with existing Benders oracles, without changing the subproblem. See
  **[the paper notes](papers/fang-2026.qmd)**.
